stimulus.text:
Electoral votes for president, election of 1800 (138 electors; 70 votes needed to win). Each elector cast two votes, one for each of two men, without naming which man was his choice for president and which for vice president.

| Candidate | Party | Electoral votes |
| Thomas Jefferson | Democratic-Republican | 73 |
| Aaron Burr | Democratic-Republican | 73 |
| John Adams | Federalist | 65 |
| Charles Cotesworth Pinckney | Federalist | 64 |
| John Jay | Federalist | 1 |

The tie sent the election to the House of Representatives, which chose Jefferson on the 36th ballot in February 1801.
stimulus.source_note: Electoral vote totals from the National Archives, 1800 Electoral College Results. Public record.

source: original; stimulus table drawn from the National Archives, 1800 Electoral College Results.
stem: Why was a tie between Jefferson and Burr possible in 1800?

options.text: Each state cast only one vote in the Electoral College.
options.misconception: Background: each state had as many electors as it had members of Congress, not one vote.

options.text: The House of Representatives chose the electors for each state.
options.misconception: Background: the states chose their own electors; the House did not choose them.

options.text: Each elector cast two unnamed votes, one for each of two men.
The candidates had to win a majority of the popular vote first.
options.misconception: Background: the president was chosen by electors, not by a popular-vote majority.

rationales.C: The stimulus says each elector cast two votes, one for each of two men, without naming which was for president and which for vice president.
rationales.A: The states did not cast one vote each.
rationales.B: The House did not choose the electors.
rationales.D: A popular-vote majority was not the rule.
rationales.general:
1. The stimulus explains the old rule: each elector cast two votes, one for each of two men.
2. Neither vote was labeled president or vice president.
3. Background: Democratic-Republican electors all voted for both Jefferson and Burr, so both men finished with 73 votes.
4. So the tie was built into the rules: the system could not tell the two running mates apart.
Remember: when a tie looks strange, read the voting rule; the rule usually explains it.
